summary: Defines the format of electronic signatures that stay valid over long periods, including evidence that holds up even if the signer later denies it. It was replaced by RFC 5126.

eli5.summary: It is a way to sign a paper so that many years later you can still prove it was really signed.

questions: how to keep signatures valid for years
subtitle: A format for digital signatures that remain valid and provable over many years, protecting against repudiation.

tldr.problem: Digital signatures can expire or become invalid when certificates age or cryptographic algorithms weaken. If a signer later denies creating a signature, proving its validity years later becomes difficult or impossible.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines layered signature formats starting with a base electronic signature (ES) and adding time-stamps and validation data (certificates, revocation information) to create time-stamped (ES-T) and complete (ES-C) versions. Archive time-stamps can re-protect older signatures against future algorithm weakness.
tldr.outcome: Long-term electronic signatures can be validated and verified even years later, with evidence that holds up in arbitration even if the signer attempts to deny creating the document. This RFC was replaced by RFC 5126.

facts.label: Base cryptography
facts.value: Public key cryptography with X.509 certificates

facts.label: Revocation info
facts.value: Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) or OCSP responses

facts.label: Arbitration capable
facts.value: ES-C form with timestamp provides evidence

facts.label: Long-term renewal
facts.value: ES-A can be re-time-stamped with stronger algorithms

today: RFC 3126 was replaced by RFC 5126, which refined and expanded the long-term signature format to reflect experience with deployment and evolving cryptographic standards.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3126 defines formats for electronic signatures that remain valid over long periods, with evidence protecting against repudiation (when a signer later denies creating the signature). Electronic signatures can be used in business transactions—like purchase orders, contracts and invoices—where years later, disputes may arise and validation must still be possible.

The RFC uses public key cryptography and X.509 certificates for authentication. Key innovation is the use of Time-Stamping Authorities (TSAs) and Trusted Service Providers (TSPs) to provide time-stamps and maintain validation data. A signature policy defines the technical and procedural requirements for creation, validation and verification in a particular business context.
sections.eli5: Electronic signatures need extra layers to stay trustworthy over time, like adding time-stamps from trusted authorities and keeping records of certificates and status checks.

sections.title: Signature Layers and Validation Data
sections.content:
The RFC defines three progressively stronger signature forms. The Electronic Signature (ES) is the basic signature: the signer's digital signature over the data, the signature policy identifier and other signed attributes (like signing time). It provides authentication and integrity protection but does not prove timing.

An ES-T (ES with Time-Stamp) adds a time-stamp over the digital signature from a TSA. This proves the signature existed at a specific time and helps prevent repudiation of existence. An ES-C (ES with Complete validation data) includes references to all certificates in the chain and all revocation information (certificate revocation lists or CRLs) available at that time. The ES-C enables arbitration because a third party can later validate the signature against the archived data.

Signers must provide at least the ES form, though ES-T or ES-C is preferred. If not provided by the signer, verifiers should create ES-T immediately upon first receipt, or maintain secure time records, to protect against later repudiation claims.
sections.eli5: A simple signature is just your name. Adding a time-stamp proves when you signed. Adding the notary's records and certificate information lets someone prove it years later even if you deny it.

sections.title: Extended and Archive Validation Data
sections.content:
An ES-X (ES with eXtended validation data) extends the ES-C by adding actual certificate and revocation information values (instead of just references) when the verifier may not have access to them. This is called X-Long form. To protect against future algorithm weakness, Type 1 X-Time-Stamp time-stamps all the validation data together, while Type 2 X-Time-Stamp time-stamps individual reference data separately. A combination creates X-Long-Time-Stamped format.

Before algorithms or certificates used in ES-C time-stamps become weak, the entire signature and validation data should be re-time-stamped as Archive Validation Data (ES-A) using stronger algorithms if available. This process can be repeated before each time-stamp certificate expires or algorithm weakens, creating multiple embedded time-stamps that extend the signature's validity indefinitely.
sections.eli5: As time goes on and security weaknesses appear, you can add new time-stamps with better security, like refreshing the notary seal on old documents.

sections.title: Components and Structure
sections.content:
An electronic signature consists of several components: a signature policy (identifying the rules for creation and validation), the signed user data (what is being signed), a digital signature (the cryptographic signature), and signed attributes (like signing time and signer location). The signature policy may define required attributes such as the signer's commitment type (approval, receipt, creation) and signer location (the jurisdiction or device location at signing time).

Validation data includes certificates in the certification path, revocation status information showing whether certificates were valid at the time of signing, and time-stamps from TSAs. The signature can include multiple signatures over the same data (independent signatures) or signatures of signatures (counter-signatures for approval chains).
sections.eli5: The signature package includes who signed it, what they signed, when, what they committed to, plus all the official records needed to prove it was valid at that time.

sections.title: Validation Process and Arbitration
sections.content:
To validate a signature, the verifier checks the digital signature against the signed data and attributes, confirms the signing time matches the time-stamp, verifies the signer's certificate was valid at that time by checking revocation status (CRL or OCSP), and verifies the certification path back to a trusted root. If the signature is ES-T or ES-C, the verifier can check that validation data was accurate at the time of the time-stamp.

For arbitration, if a signer later claims the signature is invalid, an arbitrator can validate the ES-C using the archived certificates and revocation information. The signature policy defines what the signer committed to. If the signer denies signing, the time-stamp provides evidence that the signature existed at a specific time. The arbitrator verifies the signature and all supporting validation data are correct according to the signature policy, and decides accordingly.
sections.eli5: To check a signature later, you verify the math works, check that the signer's certificate was good at signing time, and compare everything against the policy rules.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Conformance
sections.content:
Signers must protect their private keys from compromise. The RFC builds on RFC 2459 (X.509 PKI), RFC 2630 (CMS Cryptographic Message Syntax), RFC 2634 (Enhanced Security Services), and RFC 2439 (OCSP). Choice of cryptographic algorithms should follow current security standards; algorithms that are known to be weak should not be used for new signatures.

Verifiers must support ES-C validation. Signers conforming to the RFC must produce at least an ES signature with a signature policy identifier and other required signed attributes. Verifiers using time-stamping must either create an ES-T on first receipt or keep secure time records. Verifiers using secure records (ES-C(bis)) must maintain auditable records of validation time and supporting certificates/revocation information without detectably modifying them later.
sections.eli5: Keep secret keys secret, use strong encryption, and keep accurate records. Verifiers must be able to check signatures properly and preserve evidence fairly.
